forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Vale of White Horse earned £6.401m on cash balances in 2025/26 against a £4.342m budget, with no borrowing
news_drafts.lead:
Vale of White Horse District Council earned £6.401m in interest on its cash balances in 2025/26, £2.059m more than the £4.342m it budgeted, according to the outturn report (the actual figures for a year once it has ended) put to the Joint Audit and Governance Committee. Including property investments and loans outside treasury management, total investment income was £6.587m against a budget of £4.426m.

The report says the Bank of England base rate fell by three quarter-point cuts during the year, to 3.75 per cent in March 2026, more slowly than forecast, so deposits earned more than budgeted. After 3.3 per cent inflation, the real return on investments was 0.92 per cent. The council did not need to borrow during the year, and the report says it and South Oxfordshire, with which it shares officers and this committee, "continue to take a prudent approach to their debt strategy". Both stayed within the limits and prudential indicators (the measures every council must publish to show its borrowing is affordable) set in February 2025.

Internal audit's picture is mixed. Its opinion on 2024/25 was a satisfactory system of governance, risk and internal control. All eight key financial audits, including treasury management, council tax and payroll, were rated Substantial assurance, with five minor actions between them. A cyber security audit, covering artificial intelligence, was rated Limited assurance, with nine actions, two of them Priority 1, the most serious category. Eight Priority 1 actions are overdue as of 25 September 2026, and 67 of 131 open audit actions are past due. The committee's annual report calls the number of overdue recommendations "excessive" and says recent reports show it falling.

On the external audit, Bishop Fleming disclaimed the 2024/25 accounts for both councils, meaning it did not give an opinion. Its roadmap aims for qualified accounts for 2025/26 and unqualified for 2026/27. Three audits were deferred from the 2025/26 plan: two pending the Ocella replacement project, and one moved to 2027/28.

news_drafts.headline: Vale of White Horse investment returns ahead of budget as deposit rates beat forecast
news_drafts.lead: The Vale of White Horse council expects to receive £1.146m more in investment income than budgeted for 2026–27, driven by higher returns on its treasury deposits, the cabinet heard this week. The council's cash reserves are earning 4.26 per cent on average, outperforming the government's Sterling Overnight Index Average benchmark of 3.74 per cent. However, the council is also forecasting a £698,000 overspend on employee costs in the first quarter, largely because of spending on staff for the local government reorganisation programme, project surveyors and temporary legal cover. A £0.7m underspend on disabled facilities grants, which fund home adaptations for disabled people, is under national review by the Department for Health and Social Care, and the council risks having to return unspent money.

findings.paper_title: VALE Cabinet budget setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: If Local Government Reorganisation proceeds with April 2028 vesting as originally planned, capital projects may be subject to Secretary of State restrictions
findings.detail: If LGR vests on 1 April 2028 as originally intended, the Secretary of State may issue Section 24 directions that could restrict capital projects. The scope of these restrictions is unknown as the Secretary of State's discretion is very wide. The council cannot plan for specific restrictions at this stage.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand potential constraints on the council's capital spending that could affect asset maintenance and service delivery; this creates uncertainty around project completion and timing.
findings.quote: If that is the case, then capital projects may be subject to further restrictions which officers are unable to advise on at this time as the discretion of the Secretary of State is extremely wide in this regard.

findings.paper_title: VALE Cabinet budget setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: Three million pounds set aside in reserves for Local Government Reorganisation implementation, with allocation still being determined
findings.detail: The council has set aside £3.0m in reserves to cover transitional costs related to LGR implementation. The work to allocate these funds to specific purposes is ongoing. This reduces reserves available to support the revenue budget.
findings.matters: A material one-off provision drawn from reserves reduces the available buffer for future budget shortfalls and compounds the reserve sustainability challenge identified in the MTFP.
findings.quote: A provision of £3.0 million has been set aside in reserves and work continues to identify how these funds will be allocated.

findings.paper_title: VALE Cabinet budget setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: Managed vacancy factor of £250k cannot be achieved due to high staff retention, requiring review
findings.detail: The council budgeted for £250k in savings from managed vacancies (not filling vacancies to save money). However, staff retention has been higher than expected, preventing the council from achieving this saving. The factor will be reviewed.
findings.matters: If budgeted vacancy savings cannot be achieved, this indicates a structural overspend in payroll that must be addressed through other savings, service changes, or accepted as higher than planned costs.
findings.quote: the managed vacancy factor was reduced to £250,000, but we are still seeing a high level of staff retention which means the council has been unable to meet this level and therefore it will be reviewed further.

findings.paper_title: VALE Cabinet budget setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: Pay award calculated at 3.8 per cent but budgeted at 3 per cent, pending UNISON agreement
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget assumed a 3% pay award. Pay negotiations have resulted in a calculated settlement of 3.8%, which is 0.8 percentage points higher. This increase is subject to final agreement with UNISON.
findings.matters: Pay is typically 50%+ of a council's budget; a 0.8% variance on a large payroll base is material and must be funded from elsewhere or accepted as an overspend.
findings.quote: the pay award for 2026/27 was anticipated to be three per cent, as per the pay agreement this has been calculated as 3.8 per cent but is subject to negotiation with UNISON.

findings.paper_title: VALE Cabinet budget setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: A one per cent change in average interest rates could swing annual investment income by more than £1m, with rates currently higher than originally budgeted
findings.detail: The council's budget includes projected investment income based on assumed interest rates and available balances. In the current economic climate, interest rates are remaining higher than expected when the 2026/27 budget was set. This creates material income volatility: a 1% movement in average rates could change annual investment income by more than £1m.
findings.matters: Investment income is a material component of budget balance; this volatility creates material planning risk and could require compensating savings if rates fall, or enable additional spending if rates rise.
findings.quote: In the changing economic climate interest rates are continuing to remain higher than expected and by way of illustration, a one per cent change in the average interest rate on investments could result in more than a £1 million change in investment income over a year.

daily_post.headline: Disabled Facilities Grant underspend of £0.7m under national department review, with risk of clawback
daily_post.lead: A national review of DFG underspends raises the risk of clawback or reduced future allocations, which could constrain the council's ability to support disabled residents' adaptations and may signal funding pressure across the sector.
